title: How do you implement retries + DLT declaratively with `@RetryableTopic` (automatic retry topics with increasing backoff → DLT), how is a retry topic different from the DLT, and how do you prevent infinite retry loops (bounded attempts + classify transient vs permanent failures)?
shortTitle: How do you implement retries and a dead letter topic declaratively with @RetryableTopic?

s1_definition.profdef: `@RetryableTopic` is a Spring Kafka annotation that implements non-blocking retries by automatically creating a series of dedicated retry topics and a final dead letter topic. When a listener throws, the record is forwarded to the next retry topic rather than retried in place, each retry topic applies an increasing backoff, and after the configured number of attempts the record lands in the dead letter topic. A retry topic is a temporary holding stage where the record will be reprocessed after a delay, whereas the dead letter topic is the terminal parking lot for records that exhausted all attempts. You prevent infinite loops by bounding the attempts and by classifying exceptions so permanent failures skip retries entirely.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture National Bank of India processing a transfer that fails because a downstream service is briefly busy. Instead of the clerk standing at the counter re-trying the same form over and over and blocking the whole line, `@RetryableTopic` moves that form to a sequence of waiting rooms: a one-second room, then a two-second room, then a four-second room. Each waiting room gives the downstream service more time to recover before the next attempt. If the form still cannot be processed after all the waiting rooms, it goes to the permanent problem desk, the dead letter topic, so a human can look at it. The waiting rooms are retry stages; the problem desk is the final resting place.
s1_definition.oneliner: `@RetryableTopic` gives non-blocking retries through separate retry topics with growing backoff ending in a dead letter topic, where retry topics reprocess after a delay and the dead letter topic is terminal.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `@RetryableTopic` is a Spring Kafka annotation that implements non-blocking retries by automatically creating a series of dedicated retry topics and a final dead letter topic. When a listener throws, the record is forwarded to the next retry topic rather than retried in place, each retry topic applies an increasing backoff, and after the configured number of attempts the record lands in the dead letter topic. A retry topic is a temporary holding stage where the record will be reprocessed after a delay, whereas the dead letter topic is the terminal parking lot for records that exhausted all attempts. You prevent infinite loops by bounding the attempts and by classifying exceptions so permanent failures skip retries entirely.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture National Bank of India processing a transfer that fails because a downstream service is briefly busy. Instead of the clerk standing at the counter re-trying the same form over and over and blocking the whole line, `@RetryableTopic` moves that form to a sequence of waiting rooms: a one-second room, then a two-second room, then a four-second room. Each waiting room gives the downstream service more time to recover before the next attempt. If the form still cannot be processed after all the waiting rooms, it goes to the permanent problem desk, the dead letter topic, so a human can look at it. The waiting rooms are retry stages; the problem desk is the final resting place.

**One line to remember:** `@RetryableTopic` gives non-blocking retries through separate retry topics with growing backoff ending in a dead letter topic, where retry topics reprocess after a delay and the dead letter topic is terminal.

sections.s2_technical:
The classic in-place retry done by DefaultErrorHandler is blocking: while it retries a record with backoff, the consumer thread for that partition is held, so every record behind it waits too. `@RetryableTopic` makes retries non-blocking by moving the failed record off the main topic onto a dedicated retry topic and letting the main consumer continue immediately with the next record. A separate consumer reads the retry topic after the backoff delay and reprocesses the record, and if it fails again it moves to the next retry topic with a longer delay. This keeps the main partition flowing while still giving failing records their retries.

You enable it with a single annotation on the listener, for example `@RetryableTopic(attempts = "4", backoff = @Backoff(delay = 1000, multiplier = 2.0), dltStrategy = DltStrategy.FAIL_ON_ERROR)` above a method that also has `@KafkaListener(topics = "txn.events")`. Spring then auto-creates topics named like `txn.events-retry-0`, `txn.events-retry-1`, `txn.events-retry-2`, and `txn.events-dlt`. The first failure forwards to retry-0, processed after one second; the next failure to retry-1 after two seconds; then retry-2 after four seconds; and a final failure sends it to the dead letter topic. You can optionally write a method annotated with `@DltHandler` to process whatever lands in the dead letter topic, for example to persist it for triage.

The difference between a retry topic and the dead letter topic is purpose and finality. A retry topic is a transient stage whose records are expected to be reprocessed and, hopefully, to succeed on a later attempt once a transient problem clears. The dead letter topic is the end of the line; records there have failed every attempt and will not be retried automatically, so they are kept for human inspection, alerting, and possibly manual replay. Having separate retry topics per delay level is what makes the backoff non-blocking, because each level has its own consumer that simply waits the appropriate time before reading.

Preventing infinite loops relies on two controls. First, bounded attempts: the `attempts` value is a hard cap, so a record can only pass through a fixed number of retry topics before being sent to the dead letter topic, which guarantees termination. Second, exception classification: you list which exceptions are not retryable with `@RetryableTopic(exclude = { ValidationException.class, DeserializationException.class })` or include only specific retryable ones, so a permanent failure like an invalid account number is sent straight to the dead letter topic without wasting any retry stages. The senior nuances are that non-blocking retries change ordering, because a retried record is reprocessed later than records that came after it on the main topic, so you only use this where strict per-key ordering is not required; that each retry topic needs partitions and consumers, so there is operational overhead; that you must still keep processing idempotent because a record can be delivered more than once across the stages; and that blocking retries via DefaultErrorHandler remain the better choice when you must preserve ordering and the expected recovery is very fast.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem at National Bank of India is that a transfer enrichment step calls a downstream fraud-scoring service that is occasionally slow, and blocking retries on the main topic were stalling the whole settlement flow.

Problem 1 — when the fraud-scoring service was briefly overloaded, the listener threw, and the in-place retry held the partition for several seconds per record, so a backlog built up and even healthy transfers for Priya were delayed. This is exactly what non-blocking `@RetryableTopic` solves: the failing record is moved to a retry topic and the main flow keeps moving.

Problem 2 — the team needed the retries to space out so the fraud service had time to recover, not hammer it immediately. This is exactly what the increasing backoff across retry topics solves: one second, then two, then four seconds between attempts.

Problem 3 — some failures are permanent, like a malformed account number that will never validate, and retrying those is pointless and risks an endless loop. This is exactly what bounded attempts plus exception classification solves: cap the attempts so termination is guaranteed, and send validation failures straight to the dead letter topic.

The code will define a TxnEvent, a listener that throws a transient scoring error a couple of times then succeeds and throws a permanent validation error for a bad account, a `RetryableTopicSim` that forwards failures across retry stages with growing backoff and finally to the dead letter topic, and a `DltHandlerSim` that records terminal failures. The demo step is: process a transfer that recovers after two retry stages, and a transfer with an invalid account that is classified permanent and goes straight to the dead letter topic, while the main flow is never blocked.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql (Flyway migration)
CREATE TABLE settlements (
    txn_id     VARCHAR(30) PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    amount     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL,
    settled_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE TABLE dead_letters (
    id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    txn_id        VARCHAR(30),
    reason        VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    failed_at     TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: localhost:9092
    consumer:
      group-id: settlement
      auto-offset-reset: earliest
bank:
  retry:
    attempts: 4            # main + 3 retry stages, then DLT
    initial-backoff-ms: 1000
    multiplier: 2.0        # 1s, 2s, 4s
```

sections.s5_journey:
The input is two transfer events: TXN-1 for Rajesh, which fails transiently twice before succeeding, and TXN-2 with a bad account, which fails permanently.

Step 1: TXN-1 is processed on the main topic and the fraud-scoring service is busy, so the listener throws a transient exception. Instead of blocking the partition, the record is forwarded to retry-0 with a one-second backoff, and the main flow continues immediately.

Step 2: After one second the retry-0 consumer reprocesses TXN-1, the scoring service is still busy, and it throws again. The record moves to retry-1 with a two-second backoff.

Step 3: After two seconds the retry-1 consumer reprocesses TXN-1, the scoring service has recovered, and the settlement succeeds. The record never needed the final stage, and no dead letter was produced.

Step 4: TXN-2 is processed on the main topic with account BAD-ACCT. The listener throws a validation exception, which is classified as permanent and non-retryable. The record skips every retry stage.

Step 5: TXN-2 goes straight to the dead letter topic, where the dead letter handler persists it with the reason recorded, so the operations team can investigate the invalid account.

Step 6: The final output shows TXN-1 settled after two backoffs, TXN-2 routed immediately to the dead letter topic, and a dead letter total of one, with the main flow never blocked.

sections.s6_takeaway:
`@RetryableTopic` is Spring Kafka's declarative way to get non-blocking retries ending in a dead letter topic. The key difference from in-place retries is that instead of holding the consumer thread and blocking the partition while it retries, it forwards the failing record onto a dedicated retry topic and lets the main consumer carry on immediately. Separate consumers read each retry topic after a delay, so the backoff grows across stages, and after a bounded number of attempts the record lands in the dead letter topic. I enable it with a single annotation specifying the number of attempts, the initial backoff, and a multiplier, and Spring auto-creates the retry topics and the dead letter topic for me.

The distinction an interviewer wants is between a retry topic and the dead letter topic. A retry topic is a transient holding stage where the record will be reprocessed after a delay, in the hope that a temporary problem has cleared. The dead letter topic is the end of the line, holding records that failed every attempt, which are kept for alerting, inspection, and possibly manual replay, and I can process them with a method annotated to handle the dead letter topic.

I prevent infinite retry loops with two controls. The first is bounding the attempts, which is a hard cap that guarantees a record can only traverse a fixed number of retry stages before termination in the dead letter topic. The second is classifying exceptions, so permanent failures like an invalid account number are excluded from retries and sent straight to the dead letter topic, while only genuinely transient failures like a busy downstream service go through the retry stages.

In the settlement service at National Bank of India this fixed a real pain point where our fraud-scoring call was occasionally slow and in-place retries were stalling the whole settlement flow and delaying even Priya's healthy transfers. With retry topics, a transient scoring failure for Rajesh's transfer was spaced out over one, two, and four seconds while the main flow kept moving, and it usually recovered by the second stage, whereas a transfer with a bad account was classified permanent and parked in the dead letter topic instantly. The senior nuance I always add is that non-blocking retries reorder records, because a retried record is reprocessed later than ones that followed it, so I only use this pattern where strict per-key ordering is not required, and I keep processing idempotent because a record can still be delivered more than once across the stages; when ordering must be preserved and recovery is fast, blocking retries are the better tool.

---

keyPoints: Dead Letter Topic (DLT): store failed messages for later analysis
Retry topic: automatic retry with backoff before DLT
Poison pill: message that always fails — skip or DLT
